# How the 🤿 Dive Shop was built: standards in, a unit out

*7th grade math, Unit 1 (Georgia GADOE 7.NR.1.1 to 7.NR.1.5). Made by `scripts/builder/make-report.mjs` from `docs/builder/G7-UNIT1-LOG.md` on 2026-11-01 16:31 UTC. Rerun it whenever the log grows; do not edit this file by hand.*

## In one paragraph

We gave a team of AI agents the Georgia 7th grade math standards and asked for the first unit. In 1 h 38 min of clock time (13:30 to 15:08 UTC), the team split the year into 10 units, built a working 5-station shop with 9 skills at three levels, picked 13 videos, made 5 interactive note sheets, and checked 10,800 practice problems against a second, independent solver. A game designer made Deep Dive Rescue, a game for the unit. A fresh agent took the unit test without the answer key: 324 of 324 answers matched. The agents reported 1.91 million tokens. That is not the billed total: each step re-sends the agent's work so far, so the billed amount is likely closer to 60.14 million tokens, mostly cheap cached re-reads. At API prices that is about $20.83 (between $3.92 and $25.50). Checks caught real problems along the way: a picture that gave away the answer, a crash, and 5 questions that needed better wording, then 2 more test questions to fix. The best catch came last: the answer-key checker had passed every problem, but a fresh pair of eyes found a question with two right answers, so the team upgraded the checker to look at every step and proved it works by breaking it on purpose. Each finding went back to the builder and was checked again. A person still has to approve the note sheets and click each video once.

## What went wrong and was redone

- **The picture gave away the answer.** The dive line drew the arrow before she had to say which way to move. The lead saw it in a screenshot and sent the builder back (round 2). Lesson: a person-style look at screenshots finds things scripts don't.
- **A crash.** Two problem makers (`zeroWord`, `ratWord`) could crash after round 1. The builder fixed it in round 2, and the solver found it on its own too.
- **5 questions needed better wording or numbers.** The solver flagged them; the builder applied all of them in round 3; the solver checked again with no new findings.
- **The note sheets were rebuilt.** The first version came before the owner shared his worksheet checklist. Round 2 rebuilt them to it: generated pages, hidden answers, a review packet, teacher copies, saving with backups. It cost the most tokens of any rework.
- **Videos couldn't be opened.** YouTube is blocked from the build computer, so the videographer could only confirm ids from search results. Five channels were inferred, not seen.
- **A question had two right answers, and the checker missed it.** In the Dive Log, "which two make a whole number?" had two right pairs. The independent checker passed it because it only compared the last step. The 👀 looks review found it; the builder fixed it (round 5), and the solver upgraded `check-math` to check every step and fail any choice with two right options (round 4), then proved it by breaking two solvers on purpose.
- **The blind solve found 2 questions to fix.** On some hard (L3) items the last step only asked for the sign, so a guess had a 50% chance and the fraction work was done for her. Fixed by the builder and rechecked by the solver.
- **A commit took in someone else's half-done work.** Agents share one folder; a commit picked up part of the game designer's wiring. Caught right after.

## What a person still has to do

- **Approve the note sheets.** Read the review packet (`docs/builder/WORKSHEETS-G7-DIVE-review.md`); the sheets say "A grown-up checked it: (not yet)" until then.
- **Click each video once** (13 picks, `docs/builder/VIDEOS-G7-UNIT1.md`) to see it plays, is on the right channel and fits. Start with the 5 whose channel was inferred.
- **Fill the video gaps** if wanted: no video on distance as |p − q|, none on a vertical number line, none on multi-step word problems.
- **Play the shop on a phone** and try one order per station.
- **Approve the commit and merge** the branch.

## What to change for Unit 2

- **Give every agent the owner's checklists before it starts.** The worksheet maker built twice because the checklist came after round 1.
- **Log the lead's tokens.** The coordinating session has no count, so the true total is higher than shown.
- **Ask agents to report tokens split** (input, output, cache) so the cost is one number, not a range.
- **Each agent works in its own copy of the code** (or commits only its own files) so a commit can't pick up someone else's half-done work.
- **Have the builder take a screenshot of every new picture before handing off**, and ask "does this show the answer?" The giveaway would have been caught one round sooner.
- **Let the videographer reach YouTube** (or have a person check ids during the run) so ids are confirmed, not inferred.
- **Start the solver while the builder works,** from the spec, so it is ready the minute the shop is.
- **Keep the every-step checker on from the start.** It is built now; Unit 2 gets it for free.
- **Run the looks review earlier**, right after the builder's first round. A person-style look found what the scripts missed, twice (the giveaway and the two right answers).
- **Hold the unit test at about 40% hard (L3) questions.** The blind solver noticed the engine doesn't do this yet, in any shop.
- **Never let a hard question end with a sign-only choice**: it is a coin flip and gives the work away.

## Cost: how it was worked out

Prices (Anthropic, per million tokens): input $4, output $20, cache read $0.20, cache write about $5.

*Andy runs this on a Claude plan, so this is usage against the plan, not a bill; the dollar figures are what the same work would cost at API prices. The real numbers are on the usage page.*

**The token counts in the log are what the harness reported for each agent, not the billed total.** They very likely understate it: every tool call re-sends the agent's growing context (mostly as cache reads), so an agent with 115 tool calls reads far more than its reported count.

**Billed estimate (the headline).** Each tool call re-sends the agent's context. We assume the average context per call is half of that run's reported tokens, capped at 150k (high case: all of it, same cap), and price those re-reads as cache reads at $0.20 per million. The reported tokens themselves are priced as input and output (95% at $4, 5% at $20).

| Case | How | Billed tokens | Cost at API prices |
|---|---|---|---|
| Low | Only the reported tokens, priced at the "likely" mix below (no re-reads counted) | 1.91 million | $3.92 |
| **Likely** | Re-reads: tool calls × half the run's reported tokens (at most 150k a call), as cache reads; reported tokens as input/output | about 60.14 million | **$20.83** |
| High | Same, with the full reported tokens per call (same cap) | about 83.51 million | $25.50 |

The reported counts have no input / output / cache split. Priced on their own (no re-reads), they come to:

| Mix | Assumed | $ per million tokens | Reported tokens only |
|---|---|---|---|
| Low (mostly cache reads) | 85% cache reads at $0.20, 10% fresh input at $4, 5% output at $20. Agents re-read the same files and chat history many times, and repeated reads are cached. | $1.57 | $3.00 |
| Likely (some caching) | 75% cache reads at $0.20, 10% cache writes at $5, 10% fresh input at $4, 5% output at $20. Our best guess for long agent runs. | $2.05 | $3.92 |
| High (no caching at all) | 95% input at $4 and 5% output at $20, as if nothing were cached. A ceiling, not a real case. | $4.80 | $9.19 |

**The lead** (the coordinating session) and the feature keeper it ran have no measured token count. If they used tokens at the same rate per minute as the measured agents (a guess), this is what they would add. Kept out of the totals. At 12,460 tokens per minute for 1 h 1 min, that is about 760k reported tokens, or about $8.27 in the same billed terms ($1.56 to $10.13). Even with that added at the high end, the run comes to under $36 at API prices.

**A rough comparison with a person (an assumption, not a measurement).** Our guess for one experienced teacher who can also code, working alone, sized from the pieces (9 problem makers with pictures, 5 note sheets of about 40 minutes of student work each). There is no timing data from a person doing this; treat it as a rough yardstick only. At $50 an hour:

| Task | Hours (assumed) |
|---|---|
| Read the standards, plan 10 units, write the Unit 1 spec | 4 |
| Build the shop: 5 stations, 9 skills, rewards, wiring, room | 8 |
| 9 problem generators at 3 levels, with the dive-line pictures | 22 |
| 5 interactive note sheets with checked, hidden answers | 20 |
| Find and vet 13 videos for 5 stations | 5 |
| Independent answer check, fixes, screenshots, testing | 9 |
| **Total** | **68 hours, about $3,400** |

Against that: about 1 h 38 min of clock time and $3.92 to $25.50 in tokens at API prices, plus the owner's time to review. The agents' work still needs that review; the person's would too.
